rationale: Semantically identical to the standard definition, repackaged. Wikipedia's Metric_space lists d(x,x)=0, positivity, symmetry, triangle inequality and records that non-negativity is derived; the ETSU Munkres 20 notes list 'd(x,y) >= 0 for all x,y and d(x,y)=0 if and only if x=y', symmetry, triangle. The item uses the equivalent three-axiom list with (M1) as the biconditional d(x,y)=0 iff x=y and no non-negativity axiom (it is proved as lem-metric-nonnegativity). Convention deltas: codomain is R with no +infinity value; pseudometric (Pseudometric_space: drop identity of indiscernibles) and ultrametric (Ultrametric_space: d(x,z) <= max{d(x,y),d(y,z)}) are folded into the same item. Definition, so no proof component.

The content, that non-negativity follows from the other metric axioms, is stated on Wikipedia's Metric_space ('Non-negativity is derived from positivity and symmetry rather than stated separately'). The item reformulates it as two claims about a function satisfying (M1') p(x,x)=0 and (M2), one for the triangle inequality and one for the strong triangle inequality; that split and the pseudometric/ultrametric generality are the alteration. The written proof is local (it reproduces the standard 0=p(x,x)<=p(x,y)+p(y,x)=2p(x,y) argument, but no source displaying it was located), so the proof component is ai-generated.

Ball_(mathematics) gives the open ball {x : d(x,p)<r} and closed ball {x : d(x,p)<=r} verbatim; Munkres 20 gives the epsilon-ball. Deltas: the library fixes the convention r>0 always (a ball of radius 0 or negative radius is never written), and the item bundles the sphere S(x,r)={y : d(x,y)=r} with the two balls. The listed 'immediate consequences' are one-line unfoldings of those definitions plus trichotomy, not separate claims. Definition, so no proof component.

Munkres 20 (ETSU notes): 'A subset A of X is bounded if there is some number M such that d(a1,a2) <= M for every pair a1,a2 in A. If A is bounded and nonempty, the diameter of A is diam(A) = sup{d(a1,a2)}' - the same diameter, with the same nonempty-and-bounded scope. Hausdorff_distance gives d(a,B) := inf_{b in B} d(a,b), the point-to-set distance, and the set-to-set infimum. Deltas: the library defines bounded by containment in a ball (equivalent for nonempty A, and it declares the empty set bounded outright), and it refuses an infinite diameter because there is no extended real line here. Definition, so no proof component.

Triangle_inequality states the metric-space reverse triangle inequality as '|d(A,C) - d(B,C)| <= d(A,B)', which is the item's statement with (A,B,C) renamed (x,y,z); same hypotheses (a metric space, three arbitrary points), same direction, no added strength. The two-line proof is written locally in the library's step format.

Hausdorff_distance states that with d(a,B):=inf_{b in B} d(a,b) the map x -> d(x,B) is 1-Lipschitz; Lipschitz_continuity supplies the constant-K definition. The item states the same fact as the explicit inequality |d(x,A)-d(y,A)| <= d(x,y) and carries the nonemptiness hypothesis on A explicitly, because in this library inf of the empty set is undefined; that explicitness is the alteration. Proof written locally.

Open_set gives the metric-space definition verbatim: 'a subset U is open if for any point x in U, there exists a real number epsilon > 0 such that any point y satisfying d(x,y) < epsilon belongs to U', and defines a closed set as the complement of an open set; Munkres 20 Lemma 20.B is the same criterion. The item adds only the name of the collection T_d and the word clopen. Definition, so no proof component.

That |x-y| is the usual metric on R, that its balls are the open intervals (x-r,x+r) and that this induces the usual topology is standard and is the n=1 case of the Euclidean metric of Munkres 20; Metric_space carries the absolute-value metric as its first example. The alteration is claim 4 in the library's own convention: R is unbounded in this metric and therefore has no diameter at all, rather than diameter +infinity, and the closed-ball identity [x-r,x+r] is added. Proof written locally; the Remarks correctly note the Archimedean witness of step 1.6 is a convenience, not a necessity.

Lp_space defines the p-norms on R^n including the maximum norm; Munkres 20 defines the Euclidean metric and the square metric rho(x,y)=max|x_i-y_i| on R^n and proves the square metric's triangle inequality by the same argument as step 1.8. That d_1, d_2, d_infinity are metrics is standard. Deltas: R^n is defined ZFC-natively as the set of functions from the von Neumann natural n to R, and the hypothesis n >= 1 is carried explicitly because d_infinity would be a maximum over an empty index set at n=0. Proof written locally, and deliberately routed through Minkowski at p=1 and Cauchy-Schwarz rather than Minkowski at p=2.

Uniform_norm gives the supremum metric d(f,g)=sup_x d_Y(f(x),g(x)) on bounded functions and states it is a metric on that space. Deltas: the codomain is R rather than a general metric space, S is required nonempty, and the item explains why unbounded functions are excluded (no extended real line here). Proof written locally.

Open_set states that arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets are open and that open balls are open; Munkres 20 Lemma 20.A is exactly the item's step 1.1, with the same radius r-d(x,y). The alteration is the packaging of four claims into one theorem, including 'closed balls are closed', which is standard but is proved here from the reverse triangle inequality. Proof written locally.

Every clause matches a standard sourced definition: adherent point ('every neighbourhood of x contains a point of S'), limit point ('every neighbourhood of x contains at least one point of S different from x itself') and derived set, isolated point, interior as the largest open subset, boundary as closure minus interior with dS = d(X\S), and dense. The alteration is that all six are specialised to metric balls and bundled into one item; the two proved observations inside it (the interior is the largest open subset; the two descriptions of the boundary agree) are the sourced facts, verified here from the ball form. Definition, so no proof component.

Closure_(topology) carries all three characterisations separately: 'cl S is the smallest closed set containing S', the closure is S together with its limit points, and in a metric space x is a point of closure of S when 'the distance d(x,S) := inf{d(x,s) : s in S} = 0', plus 'S is closed if and only if S = cl S'. The alteration is bundling them into one theorem and carrying the hypothesis A nonempty on the distance characterisation only, since d(x,A) is undefined for empty A here. Proof written locally.

Limit_of_a_sequence gives metric convergence as: for each real epsilon > 0 there is N such that d(x_n,x) < epsilon for all n >= N. The item defines x_k -> p as d(x_k,p) -> 0 in R in the sense of the library's def-real-limit, which quantifies over RATIONAL epsilon and indexes from 0; those two conventions, and the recorded fact that rational and real tolerances agree, are the alteration. Definition, so no proof component.

Limit_of_a_sequence states for metric spaces: 'When it exists, the limit of a sequence is unique, as distinct points are separated by some positive distance, so for epsilon less than half this distance, sequence terms cannot be within a distance epsilon of both points.' That is the item's statement and its argument. The proof is ai-altered rather than literature-derived because the halving is rebuilt in the library's own terms and the passage from a real to a rational tolerance is inserted to fit the local convergence convention.

First-countable_space states 'every metric space is first-countable' and exhibits the countable local base at x as 'the set of open balls centered at x with radius 2^-n for all natural numbers n'. The item uses the radii 1/n for n >= 1 instead, defines neighbourhood base and first countable inline (neither notion exists elsewhere in the library yet), and states countability as 'at most countable' because the family can be finite. The proof follows the sourced argument with the reciprocal Archimedean property supplying the index.

Closure_(topology): in first-countable spaces 'cl S is the set of all limits of all convergent sequences of points in S'; Sequential_space gives sequentially closed and the fact that in first-countable spaces sequentially closed sets are closed; Axiom_of_countable_choice states that 'Every accumulation point of a subset of a metric space is a limit of a sequence of points from the subset' is equivalent to AC_omega, which is exactly the choice the item spends and flags at step 1.2. The alteration is the two-claim packaging and the explicit choice bookkeeping. Proof written locally, with the radii shifted to 1/(n+1) because N contains 0 here.

Hausdorff_space states 'all metric spaces are Hausdorff' and gives the same witness: 'using balls of radius d(x,y)/2 centered at each point creates the necessary separation, since these balls cannot overlap'. The item's statement is that pair of balls being disjoint, with the same radius. The proof adapts that sourced argument into the library's step format, adding the explicit halving justification.

Continuous_function gives the epsilon-delta definition of continuity at a point between metric spaces in exactly the item's form, and the neighbourhood formulation which is the item's ball restatement f[B(a,delta)] subset B(f(a),epsilon). The quantifier-order note (delta may depend on the point) is the source's own distinction from uniform continuity. Definition, so no proof component.

Continuous_function carries (a) the epsilon-delta condition, (b) 'the preimage of every open set is open' as the topological characterisation, and (d) the sequential characterisation for metric spaces. Conditions (c) preimages of closed sets are closed and (e) f[cl A] subset cl f[A] are the remaining clauses of the standard equivalence (Munkres, Topology, Theorem 18.1; no open-access URL for that theorem was located). The alteration is the five-way bundle and the explicit statement of where countable choice is spent, which no source states. Proof written locally.

Isometry gives the distance-preserving condition d_X(a,b)=d_Y(f(a),f(b)) and reserves 'isometry' for the bijective case, which is the item's split between isometric embedding and isometry. Subspace_topology states that restricting the metric to a subset induces the subspace topology and that its balls are intersections of ambient balls with the subset, which is the item's B_A(a,r)=B_X(a,r) cap A. The alteration is bundling the three notions into one item. Definition, so no proof component.

Isometry states 'an isometry is automatically injective' and that a bijective isometry has an isometric inverse, establishing a topological embedding onto the image; Subspace_topology supplies the target topology. The item states the same content as four explicit claims, including the ball identity f[B_X(x,r)] = B_Z(f(x),r) and the bijection between the two topologies, which is the alteration. Proof written locally.

Equivalence_of_metrics defines topologically equivalent ('they generate the same topology on X'), uniformly equivalent, and 'strongly or bilipschitz equivalent' by 'there exist positive constants alpha and beta such that, for every x,y in X, alpha d1(x,y) <= d2(x,y) <= beta d1(x,y)' - the item's Lipschitz condition verbatim. Deltas: the item says 'Lipschitz equivalent' where the source says strongly/bilipschitz (the item itself records that naming fork), and it writes uniform equivalence out in full epsilon-delta form because uniform continuity has no definition in the library yet. Definition, so no proof component.

Equivalence_of_metrics states 'Strong equivalence implies topological equivalence, but not conversely' and that uniformly equivalent metrics need not be strongly equivalent, i.e. the same three-level ranking. The item factors that into the two implications Lipschitz => uniform and uniform => topological, and explicitly declines to claim strictness (the witnesses are on the companion page). Proof written locally.

Munkres 20 Theorem 20.1 (ETSU notes): 'Let X be a metric space with metric d. Define d-bar by d-bar(x,y)=min{d(x,y),1}. Then d-bar is a metric that induces the same topology as d.' The item strengthens 'same topology' to 'uniformly equivalent' (which implies it, via thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy), adds the second standard construction d/(1+d), and adds the diameter bound diam <= 1; those additions are the alteration and each is verified in the item's own steps. Proof written locally.

Every convention claim in the remark is sourced. Pseudometric_space: a pseudometric drops the identity of indiscernibles, and 'the term semimetric space (which has a different meaning in topology) is sometimes used as a synonym, especially in functional analysis' - exactly the live naming fork the remark records. Metric_space: non-negativity is derivable, and some authors write the codomain as [0,infinity). Ultrametric_space: the strong triangle inequality. The remark's own contribution is the library-policy part (why extended metrics are not built here), which is a statement about this library, not a mathematical claim about metric spaces. Remark, so no proof component.

Ball_(mathematics) states the refuted claim and its failure explicitly: 'it is not always the case that the closure of the open ball equals the closed ball', with the discrete-metric witness where B_1(p) has closure {p} while B_1[p]=X. The item states the same false claim and keeps the surviving inclusion. Delta: it uses the subspace {0} union [1,2] of R as its witness rather than a discrete space; that space is itself the standard example of a set with an isolated point (Isolated_point lists 'S = {0} union [1,2]'). Refutation written locally.

The falsity is immediate from Munkres 20 Theorem 20.1 (every metric space carries min{d,1}, a bounded metric inducing the same topology) together with the unboundedness of R, and Bounded_set records that 'the word bounded makes no sense in a general topological space without a corresponding metric'. The alteration is the false-statement packaging: no source states it as a named false claim. Refutation written locally.

Lp_space states the comparisons in the same constants: '||x||_2 <= ||x||_1', '||x||_1 <= sqrt(n) ||x||_2' and the general '||x||_p <= ||x||_r <= n^(1/r - 1/p) ||x||_p', which at (r,p)=(1,infinity) and (2,infinity) give ||x||_inf <= ||x||_1 <= n ||x||_inf and ||x||_inf <= ||x||_2 <= sqrt(n) ||x||_inf, the item's three chains. Munkres 20 Theorem 20.3 gives the same-topology conclusion for the euclidean and square metrics. The alteration is stating the comparisons as Lipschitz equivalence of metrics with explicit constants in the library's vocabulary. Verification written locally.

Discrete_space gives the discrete metric (0 if x=y, 1 otherwise), the open-ball computation 'if r <= 1: B(x,r)={x}; if r>1: B(x,r)=X', and that every subset is open, hence clopen; Munkres 20 Example 1 is the same. The alteration is the added closed-ball and sphere computations, B-bar(x,r)={x} for 0<r<1 and X for r>=1 and S(x,1)=X minus {x}, which the sources do not compute and which the item verifies itself. Verification written locally.

Uniform_norm supplies the supremum metric on bounded functions. The two recorded facts are routine, directly checkable consequences: that the constants form an isometric copy of R (immediate from d_infinity(c-hat,c'-hat)=|c-c'|, an isometric embedding in the sense of the sourced definition) and that the supremum need not be attained, witnessed by f(k)=1-1/(k+1) against 0. Both are standard textbook observations about l-infinity; the specific witness is the item's own but is elementary and verified in its steps. Verification written locally.

P-adic_number gives v_p(a/b)=v_p(a)-v_p(b), |x|_p = p^(-v_p(x)) with |0|_p=0, and the strong triangle inequality |x+y|_p <= max{|x|_p,|y|_p}; Ultrametric_space states both further claims verbatim: 'every triple of points in the space forms an isosceles triangle' and 'Every point inside a ball is one of its centers', and records that the p-adic absolute value gives an ultrametric on Q. The alteration is the specialisation to p=2 and the deliberate development of the valuation from parity (every nonzero integer is 2^j u with u odd) instead of unique factorisation, so that the item does not rest on the primes page. Verification written locally.

PlanetMath's SNCF metric, Definition 1, is 'd_P(x,y) := 0 if x=y; d(x,P)+d(P,y) otherwise', which with P=0 in Euclidean R^n is exactly the item's rho(x,y)=||x||+||y|| for x != y. Isolated_point supplies the isolated-point notion used in claims 2 and 3, which are direct computations from the construction. Naming delta worth recording: PlanetMath's 'enhanced' SNCF metric (Definition 2) is the collinear-ray variant, which is a different function; the item treats 'post-office metric' and 'SNCF metric' as synonyms for Definition 1, as many sources do. Verification written locally.

Munkres 20 Theorem 20.1 gives the standard bounded metric min{d,1} and the sameness of topology, and the same notes use min{|a-b|,1} on R by name ('the standard bounded metric on R'). The item instantiates that on R and adds the exact diameter, diam(R)=1 in rho, which is its own one-line computation from rho(0,1)=1. Verification written locally.

The refuted claim and its failure are stated on Ball_(mathematics) ('it is not always the case that the closure of the open ball equals the closed ball'), with a discrete-metric witness. The item's witness is the subspace {0} union [1,2] of the real line, which is the standard isolated-point example listed on Isolated_point; the computation B_X(0,1)={0}, closure {0}, closed ball {0,1} is elementary and fully verified in the item's steps. Counterexample written locally.

Boundary_(topology) gives the boundary as closure minus interior; Discrete_space gives that every subset of a discrete metric space is clopen and computes the balls; Ball_(mathematics) records that the topological relations suggested by the names open ball, closed ball and sphere are not automatic. The witness (any set with at least two points under the discrete metric, giving empty boundary against a nonempty sphere) is the standard one and every step of the computation is elementary. Counterexample written locally.

Hausdorff_distance states the refuted claim's failure directly: 'The infimum of distances between two disjoint closed sets can equal zero, even when the sets do not intersect. This means the simple infimum-distance approach fails to satisfy metric axioms on the collection of subsets', and names the Hausdorff distance as the repair, which is what the item's Remarks say. The witness pair (the integers and {n+1/n : n >= 2}) is the classic textbook one; the item additionally proves both sets closed via a separation argument and shows every individual point-to-set distance is positive. Counterexample written locally.

Equivalence_of_metrics states that the hierarchy is strict, giving 'd1(x,y)=|x-y| and d2(x,y)=|tan(x)-tan(y)| on (-pi/2,pi/2)' as topologically but not strongly equivalent, and '|x-y| against |x^2-y^2| on [0,1]' as uniformly but not strongly equivalent. The item's claim is the topological-not-uniform level, witnessed by |x-y| against |1/x-1/y| on (0,infinity); that witness is the standard one for this level (the map x -> 1/x is a homeomorphism that is not uniformly bicontinuous near 0) but is not the source's, so the statement is recorded as an alteration rather than an exact match. Counterexample written locally.

Equivalence_of_metrics states that uniformly equivalent metrics need not be strongly (Lipschitz) equivalent; Munkres 20 Theorem 20.1 supplies the pair d and min{d,1} on R, which the item uses as its witness in place of the source's |x-y| against |x^2-y^2| on [0,1]. The argument, that alpha d <= min{d,1} with alpha > 0 would bound d by 1/alpha on an unbounded space, is elementary and fully verified in the item's steps. Counterexample written locally.

Munkres 20 Theorem 20.1 gives a bounded metric with the same topology as any given metric, which with the unboundedness of the real line is exactly this witness; Bounded_set records that boundedness needs a metric and is not a topological notion. The alteration is the counterexample packaging against the library's named false statement. Counterexample written locally.
